mutations.because: the whole judgement of the pool directory: existence, symlink, uid and mode in one condition. Every lock decision this script makes is a rename INTO that directory, so a pool that is a world-writable or somebody-else's directory is not a lock parent, it is a name other users can take. The test creates the directory and chmods it to 0775 and 0777 after the fact (mkdirSync's mode option is filtered by umask 022, so the mode asked for would never be the mode checked), and expects exit 2 with the refusal naming the variable. The uid half of this predicate is reached by the seam case, which now answers on the PARENT — the same find -user, the same pool_uid, judged first — so the owner half of the question is not left untested by the two being asked separately. Note what is NOT the mutation: dropping only the `[ -L ]` term. On Linux a symlink's own mode is 0777, so the `-perm -o+w` predicate still refuses it and the suite stays green — that is why the symlink case below is mutated by following the link instead
command: a group- or world-writable pool is refused

mutations.because: the derivation still asks the host how many processors it has and no longer asks how many workers a run may spawn — which is the whole input. A pool sized by nproc alone is one gate per thread: on midnight, 24 gates each entitled to 4 workers, or 24 gates each entitled to whatever a run asks for. The clamp above it cannot see the difference, and the ceiling is 64, so 24 is accepted as a legitimate answer. The test injects nproc (CF_GATE_TEST_NPROC) and reads the derived count back through the only place a count is observable without taking seats: CF_GATE_SLOTS=6 with GATE_HOST_WORKERS=4 on 24 processors is accepted because it agrees, while 5 and 7 are refused naming both variables. Under the mutation the derived count is 24, so the agreeing case refuses and the test fails on the case it was written for. Re-anchored in fix round 2: reading the processor count is now read_host_nproc, shared with the slots-x-workers budget check, so the division line is $HOST_NPROC rather than the local it used to be

the marker check reads as "is it there" instead of "is it 1" — the shape a reviewer mistakes for a defensive guard. It is the one check standing between two projects with different lock semantics and one shared pool: hexagen reimplementing this script with a different reclaim rule or a different slot file count would be admitted, publish its own holders, and the two would judge each other's locks with incompatible rules. The test writes 2 into `.format` and expects exit 2 naming the pool and the number; it also writes an empty marker, which is the arm that survives this mutation and which is why the mutation claims only the first

the staged beat goes back to TMPDIR, which is where it was before the pool existed and where it is a cross-device rename away from the lock. The rename then becomes copy-then-unlink, the beat is briefly absent at the name, beat_is_stale reads absent as stale, and the next acquire reclaims a lock whose holder is alive and heartbeating — on midnight, where the pool is tmpfs and TMPDIR is mergerfs. The test gives the run a TMPDIR and a GATE_LOCK_DIR in two DIFFERENT scratch directories (one directory could not tell a staged beat from one that landed in the right place), parks a refresh in CF_GATE_TEST_PAUSE_BEFORE_BEAT_MV, and reads the pool for gate.lock.beatnew.<pid> while asserting TMPDIR holds no cf-gate.beatnew*
command: the staged beat is inside the pool

mutations.because: the pool is judged THROUGH the symlink: `[ -L ]` is gone and find is given -L, so the uid and the mode are read off whatever the link points at. This is the shape an operator produces when told the pool is "wrong" and told to check where it points — and it is the cheapest forgery there is, because a link needs no write access to the parent beyond the link itself, so a pool name can be re-pointed at a directory somebody else controls between one acquire and the next. The test symlinks a 0700 directory this user owns at the pool's name and expects exit 2. It is mutated by following the link rather than by deleting the `[ -L ]` test: on Linux a symlink's own mode is 0777, so the `-perm -o+w` predicate refuses it anyway and dropping only `[ -L ]` leaves the suite green
command: a symlinked or relative GATE_LOCK_DIR is refused by name
